podcast.title: Controversial Content
podcast.body: The song "Bloodshot Eyes" is noted for trivializing intimate partner violence, a theme that might be disturbing to many listeners. "but be warned that the song trivialises intimate part of the violence in a way that many people might find disturbing."

podcast.title: Decline in Career and Death
podcast.body: Harris's hit-making career largely ended by 1953, and he virtually ceased performing by the early 1960s, finding that contemporary bands struggled to play his boogie style. Accounts of his final performances describe him as a "sad and pitiful figure." He died in 1969, reportedly due to complications from excessive drinking. "He died in 1969, after more or less drinking himself to death."

podcast.title: Departure from Millinder's Band
podcast.body: Driven by his confidence and the belief that he was undercompensated for "Who Threw the Whiskey in the Well," Harris decided to leave Lucky Millinder's band and embark on a solo career. "Harris went solo, and Lucky Millinda replaced him with a trumpet player and singer called Henry Glover."

podcast.title: Early Nickname "Mr. Blues"
podcast.body: Wynonie Harris was already known as "Mr. Blues" when Lucky Millinder first encountered him performing in Chicago and subsequently invited him to join his band. "Harris was already known as Mr Blues, when Melinda first saw him playing in Chicago and invited him to join the band."

podcast.title: Financial Success and Extravagance
podcast.body: Harris boasted of earning $1,500 a week by specifically targeting women with disposable income ("meat on their bones" and "long green stuff in their pocketbook"), rather than younger, less affluent audiences. He spent his earnings lavishly, once buying two Cadillacs and hiring two chauffeurs after receiving a $10,000 royalty check. "I star in Georgia, Texas, Alabama, Tennessee, and Missouri, and get those who have money to buy stronger stuff and my records to play while they drink it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Highly Confident Personality
podcast.body: Harris was renowned for his extreme self-confidence and self-belief, which propelled his success on stage but often led to strained personal relationships. This confidence contributed to his conviction that he was a major star deserving greater recognition and financial reward. "In case you hadn't realised yet, Wainoni Harris was never known as the most self-effacing of people, and that confidence gave him a huge amount of success on stage, but it didn't win him many friends in his personal life."

podcast.title: Joined Millinder's Band Residency
podcast.body: Upon joining Lucky Millinder's band, Harris began performing with them during their residency at the renowned Savoy venue. "Harris joined the Melinda band and started performing with them in their residency at the Savoy."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Remarkable Stage Presence
podcast.body: Wynonie Harris possessed an "astonishing stage presence," with many later commentators suggesting that Elvis Presley's iconic performances, including his hip thrusts and leg shaking, were merely a "watered down version" of what Harris had already been doing. "Lots of people who spoke about Elvis Presley in later years said that his performances, hip thrusts and leg shaking at all were just a watered down version of what Wainoni Harris had been doing."

podcast.title: Sound System Favorite
podcast.body: Wynonie Harris was a popular artist among early Jamaican sound system listeners, along with Louis Jordan, with his song "Bloodshot Eyes" being a significant hit. "Louis Jordan was a big favourite, as was Wynoni Harris."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Underpaid for Hit Song
podcast.body: Despite "Who Threw the Whiskey in the Well" becoming a massive hit, Harris received only a flat session fee of $37.50, while Lucky Millinder collected the royalties. This perceived injustice fueled Harris's belief that his vocal contributions were solely responsible for the record's success and that he could earn more independently. "It became a massive hit, and the only money Harris saw from it was a flat $37.50 session fee."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Vocal Influences
podcast.body: Harris was primarily recognized as a blues shouter, drawing inspiration from artists such as Big Joe Turner and Jimmy Rushing. However, he also possessed the versatility to perform in a more subtle style, akin to the jive singing of Cab Calloway or Louis Jordan. "He was primarily a blues shelter, inspired by people like Big Joe Turner and Jimmy Rushing, but he could also perform in a subtler style, close to the give singing of a cap-caller way or Louis Jordan."
